extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate mathematics students and researchers studying geometric/combinatorial proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted material concerns proving and applying structural theorems in geometric decomposition and incidence geometry (Hilbert's third problem, Sylvester–Gallai, graph decompositions, slope problem). It presents definitions, lemmas, necessary conditions, and proof techniques used to certify or refute equidecomposability and related combinatorial geometry statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Equidecomposable / Equicomplementable
rubrics_metrics.description: Two polyhedra P and Q are equidecomposable if they can be decomposed into finite sets of polyhedra P1,...,Pn and Q1,...,Qn such that Pi and Qi are congruent for all i. Two polyhedra are equicomplementable if there are equidecomposable polyhedra 'P and 'Q that also have decompositions involving P and Q of the form 'P = P ∪ P'_1 ∪ ... ∪ P'_m and 'Q = Q ∪ Q'_1 ∪ ... ∪ Q'_m where P'_k is congruent to Q'_k for all k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the formal notion used throughout the chapter for comparing polyhedra. The authors note Gerling's theorem (1844) that admitting reflections in congruences or not does not affect these definitions. Equidecomposability implies equicomplementability (take m = 0), but the converse is nontrivial and is the object of study (Hilbert's third problem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Segments in a decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: In any decomposition the edges of one piece may be subdivided by vertices or edges of other pieces; the pieces of this subdivision are called segments. In two dimensions any endpoint of a segment is some vertex; in three dimensions the end of a segment may also be a crossing of two edges. In any case all interior points of a segment belong to the same set of edges of pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segments are the atomic units to which integer labels ('pearls') are later assigned in the Pearl Lemma. The paragraph illustrates how segments can arise (example: a short segment inside an equilateral triangle that is intersection of two pieces but not an edge of either).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pearl Lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: If P and Q are equidecomposable, then one can place a positive numbers of pearls (that is, assign positive integers) to all the segments of the decompositions P = P1 ∪ ··· ∪ Pn and Q = Q1 ∪ ·· · ∪ Qn in such a way that each edge of a piece Pk receives the same number of pearls as the corresponding edge of Qk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: assign a variable xi to each segment in P and yj to each segment in Q. The edge-equality requirements yield a system of linear equations with integer coefficients of the form sum_{i: si ⊆ e} xi − sum_{j: s'_j ⊆ e'} yj = 0. Real positive solutions exist (take actual segment lengths), so by the Cone Lemma one gets positive integer solutions. An illustrated example (Dudeney dissection) shows a possible placement of pearls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cone Lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: If a system of homogeneous linear equations with integer coefficients has a positive real solution, then it also has a positive integer solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the solution set C = {x ∈ R^N : Ax = 0, x > 0} for integer matrix A is a rational cone; if nonempty it contains integer points. Proof approach given: pass to ¯C = {x ∈ R^N : Ax = 0, x ≥ 1}; show ¯C contains a rational point by Fourier–Motzkin elimination and the existence of a lexicographically smallest solution which must be rational when A is integral. An elementary example is provided illustrating elimination and minimal solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bricard's condition (Theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: If three-dimensional polyhedra P and Q with dihedral angles α1,...,αr respectively β1,...,βs are equidecomposable, then there are positive integers m_i, n_j and an integer k with m1 α1 + ··· + mr αr = n1 β1 + ··· + ns βs + kπ. The same holds more generally if P and Q are equicomplementable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the Pearl Lemma: place pearls on segments of both decompositions, sum the dihedral angles at pearls in P to get Σ1 = sum m_j α_j + k1 π with positive integer mj and nonnegative k1, and similarly Σ2 for Q. Congruence of corresponding pieces and the Pearl Lemma imply Σ1 = Σ2, yielding the stated equality (with k = k2 − k1). For equicomplementable case one applies the same counting across the auxiliary decompositions and accounts for differences by integer multiples of π.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle-sum accounting method with pearls
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute Σ1 (sum of all dihedral angles at all pearls in pieces of P's decomposition) by adding the dihedral angles at each pearl, counting multiplicities when an edge contains several pearls or a pearl lies in multiple pieces; similarly compute Σ2 for Q. Each segment in interior/boundary contributes π or 2π as appropriate; edges contribute their dihedral angle. Equating Σ1 and Σ2 yields Bricard's condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This bookkeeping method is the central device to convert geometric decomposability into an arithmetic relation among dihedral angles (up to integer multiples of π). It underpins the applications and examples that follow (ruling out equidecomposability by irrationality arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: Using dihedral-angle arithmetic + irrationality to rule out equidecomposability
rubrics_metrics.description: If Bricard's condition requires an identity m1 α1 + ... = n1 β1 + ... + kπ and one shows, e.g., that α/π is irrational while RHS would force rational multiples, then equidecomposability/equicomplementability is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: regular tetrahedron (dihedral angle arccos(1/3)) cannot be equidecomposable/equicomplementable with a cube (all dihedral angles π/2) because 1/π arccos(1/3) is irrational. Similar arguments for other tetrahedra use prior irrationality results (Chapter 7) to conclude non-equidecomposability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Convex polytope and halfspace/facet representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A convex polytope in R^d is the convex hull of a finite set S = {s1,...,sn}, P = conv(S) = { sum λ_i s_i : λ_i ≥ 0, sum λ_i = 1 }. Equivalently, convex polytopes are bounded solution sets of finite systems of linear inequalities P = { x ∈ R^d : A x ≤ b } where each facet corresponds to a hyperplane a_i^T x = b_i and one of the closed halfspaces bounded by that hyperplane contains P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes the algebraic/linear-inequality viewpoint used later; the text notes facets determine a minimal set of halfspaces whose intersection is P, and records that for a facet F the two halfspaces H_F^+, H_F^- satisfy that one contains P and the other doesn't—useful later in arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sylvester–Gallai Theorem (Theorem 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any configuration of n points in the plane, not all on a line, there is a line which contains exactly two of the points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kelly's proof (presented) chooses a pair (P0, l0) where P0 is a point not on line l0 with minimal distance to l0; geometric argument using metric (shortest distance) and order axioms shows l0 must contain exactly two points. The text remarks that some proofs avoid metric axioms (Coxeter shows order axioms suffice) and that the Fano plane demonstrates incidence axioms alone are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment: Axioms needed for Sylvester–Gallai
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof as given uses metric axioms (shortest distance) and order axioms (betweenness). Incidence axioms alone are insufficient (Fano plane shows configuration satisfying incidence axioms but with no 2-point line). Coxeter showed order axioms suffice; other proofs use Euler's formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is guidance on what structure of the ambient plane (metric/order/incidence) is required for the theorem and alternative proof strategies avoiding certain axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős–de Bruijn Theorem (Theorem 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let P be a set of n ≥ 3 points in the plane, not all on a line. Then the set L of lines passing through at least two points contains at least n lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction using Sylvester–Gallai: find a 2-point line ℓ0, remove one point on it and apply induction to remaining points; handle the case when the remainder is collinear (a pencil) separately. The theorem generalizes to abstract point-line systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motzkin/Conway general result on pair-unique set systems (Theorem 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be a set of n ≥ 3 elements, and let A1,...,Am be proper subsets of X, such that every pair of elements of X is contained in precisely one set Ai. Then m ≥ n holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs given: a short combinatorial proof (Motzkin/Conway) using counts rx (the number of sets Ai containing x) leading to a contradiction if m < n; and a linear-algebraic proof using the incidence matrix B and the invertibility/positive-definiteness of B B^T to infer rank(B) ≥ n and hence m ≥ n. The text notes an equivalence with decomposing the complete graph K_n into cliques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: Decomposing K_n into cliques ↔ set-system condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Decomposing the complete graph K_n into m cliques (different from K_n) so that every edge lies in a unique clique is equivalent to the set-system statement of Theorem 3 (with vertex sets of cliques corresponding to the Ai).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This correspondence is used to rephrase combinatorial geometry statements in graph-theoretic language and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham–Pollak Theorem (Theorem 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If K_n is decomposed into complete bipartite subgraphs H1,...,Hm, then m ≥ n − 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No purely combinatorial proof known; the presented proof (Tverberg) assigns variables x_i to vertices and derives an identity for sum_{i<j} x_i x_j as sum over bipartite parts. Assuming m < n-1 yields a nontrivial solution to a linear system which leads to a contradiction via evaluating (sum c_i)^2. The argument is linear-algebraic/analytic in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix: Basic graph definitions and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: a graph G = (V,E) with edges connecting vertices; simple graphs forbid loops and multiple edges; adjacency, incidence, complete graphs K_n, complete bipartite graphs K_{m,n}, paths P_n, cycles C_n, subgraph and induced subgraph, connectedness, components, clique (complete subgraph), independent set (induced edgeless subgraph), forest, tree, bipartite graphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions are the standard terminology used throughout the chapter and are prerequisites for understanding the graph-theoretic translations of the geometric/combinatorial theorems and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slope problem theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If n ≥ 3 points in the plane do not lie on one single line, then they determine at least n − 1 different slopes, where equality is possible only if n is odd and n ≥ 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem is sharp: constructions exist for odd n ≥ 5 with exactly n − 1 slopes, and for other n there are configurations with exactly n slopes. Proof strategy: reduce to even n = 2m case, model the problem combinatorially via a periodic sequence of permutations generated by rotating a direction, then apply a counting argument on moves to show the number t of slopes (length of sequence) satisfies t ≥ n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial permutation model for slopes (construction and required properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Associate to a chosen initial direction (not a slope of the configuration) the permutation π_0 listing the points in order of their 1D projection. Rotating the direction produces a sequence π_0 → π_1 → ... → π_t with properties: (i) π_0 = 1 2 ... n and π_t = n ... 3 2 1 (a 180° rotation), (ii) t equals the number of distinct slopes, (iii) every pair i < j is switched exactly once along the sequence, (iv) every move consists in the reversal of one or more disjoint increasing substrings (corresponding to lines whose direction is passed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combinatorial model (Goodman–Pollack reduction) translates geometric slope changes into a sequence of permutation substring reversals; the rest of the proof counts how many times letters must cross a central barrier to bound t.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of moves: crossing, touching, ordinary; counting facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Moves in the permutation sequence are classified as: crossing moves (a reversed substring involves letters from both halves of a central barrier; crossing move has order d if it moves 2d letters across the barrier), touching moves (reverse a substring adjacent to but not crossing the barrier; correspond to a line with exactly m points on one side), and ordinary moves (neither touching nor crossing). Two key facts used: (1) Between any two crossing moves there is at least one touching move. (2) Between any crossing move of order d and the next touching move there are at least d − 1 ordinary moves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counting letters that cross the barrier over all crossing moves yields sum_{i=1}^c 2 d_i ≥ n (each letter must cross at least once). Using the two facts about spacing of touching/ordinary moves gives a lower bound on total moves t in terms of these d_i, leading to t ≥ n and thus proving the slope theorem.
